chunks: From him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who said:

I was present when a question was asked about a man who married a woman on the condition of one hundred dinars, on the condition that she travels with him to his country; if she does not travel with him, her dowry is fifty dinars. I was asked: What do you think if she does not travel with him to his country? He said: If he wants to take her to the land of polytheism (Bilad al-Shirk), there is no condition binding her regarding that, and she is entitled to the one hundred dinars he bestowed upon her. And if he wants to take her to the land of Muslims and the abode of Islam, then he has what he stipulated upon her, for Muslims are bound by their conditions. And he is not permitted to take her to his country until he pays her her dowry, or she is content with what she is content with, and that is permissible for him.

key_terms.الْمُسْلُونَ عِنْدَ شُرُوطِهِمْ: Muslims are bound by their conditions

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a conditional dowry if the wife relocates to a land of polytheism versus a land of Islam?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) establishes that the validity of the conditional dowry reduction hinges on the destination's religious character: if the husband relocates her to a 'land of polytheism' (Bilad al-Shirk), the condition is void and she retains the full dowry, whereas in a 'land of Islam,' the condition holds as Muslims abide by their stipulations. This ruling underscores the practical implication of *al-Muslimun 'inda shurutihim* (Muslims are bound by their conditions) while linking the wife's religious security to the geographical context of the marriage. The Imam further clarifies that relocation to a specific country requires either full dowry payment or the wife's explicit consent, ensuring her rights are not compromised by unilateral decisions.
